intro: By now you have read the major traditions one at a time: the Torah and the prophets, the Gospels and Paul, the Qur'an and the Hadith, the Upanishads and the Gita, the Dhammapada, the Analects and the Daodejing, the Guru Granth Sahib, and traditions carried in story and ceremony. This unit turns the course sideways. Instead of asking what one tradition teaches, it asks a single human question and lets each tradition answer it in its own words.

The questions are the oldest ones. How should a person live, and what do people owe one another? What happens when we die, and why is there suffering at all? Every student in the room already has some answer, from a family, a congregation, a book or their own thinking. Reading the traditions side by side shows where their answers meet, such as the Golden Rule and care for the poor. It also shows where they part, over God, the self and what comes after death.

By the end of the unit you will be able to set two or three sacred texts beside each other, attribute each teaching to its tradition, explain the reason each text gives, and show the variety inside a tradition as well as the differences between them. You will practice the discipline at the heart of this course: comparing carefully, in the traditions' own terms, without declaring a winner.
bigQuestion: When the world's traditions answer the same great questions, what do they share, where do they differ, and why?

words.d: the study of how people should live and what they owe one another
a commandment in Jewish tradition; Rabbinic tradition counts 613 in the Torah
the teaching to treat others as one would want to be treated, found in many traditions
in Hindu thought, duty, right order and the responsibilities of one's role in life
selfless service in Sikh tradition, offered to God through service to people
the Confucian virtue of humaneness or benevolence
the dead being raised to life again, in body, at the end of time
the cycle of birth, death and rebirth taught in Hindu, Buddhist, Jain and Sikh traditions
in Hindu thought, liberation from the cycle of rebirth

test.q: Which text contains the command to love your neighbor as yourself?
test.why: Leviticus 19:18 commands Israel to love the neighbor as oneself.

test.q: Which three things does Micah 6:8 say the LORD requires?
choices: To do justly, love mercy and walk humbly with God
Right speech, right action and right livelihood
test.why: Micah 6:8 names doing justly, loving mercy and walking humbly with God.

test.q: How does Confucius's rule of reciprocity differ from Matthew 7:12?
choices: Confucius states it negatively; Matthew states it positively
They are word for word the same
test.why: The Analects say do not do to others what you do not want; Matthew says do to others what you would have them do.

choices: Giving a fixed yearly share of savings to the poor and others
test.why: Zakat, one of the Five Pillars, is a required yearly gift from savings, commonly 2.5 percent.

test.q: In the Gita, what does Krishna teach about action?
choices: Do your duty without craving its reward
Avoid all action to escape karma
Act only when reward is certain
test.why: Krishna teaches karma yoga: act from duty and let go of attachment to the fruits.

test.q: Which Sikh practice serves a free meal to everyone who comes?
test.why: The langar in every gurdwara serves a free meal to all, seated as equals.

test.q: Which three steps of the Eightfold Path make up ethical conduct?
test.why: Buddhists group right speech, right action and right livelihood as sila, ethical conduct.

test.q: What distinguishes secular ethics from religious ethics?
choices: It began only in the twentieth century
It grounds its answer in reason or human nature rather than revelation
test.why: Secular ethics, such as Aristotle's, Kant's or Mill's, rests on reason and experience rather than on God or karma.

test.q: Which statement about Judaism and life after death is accurate?
choices: Jewish movements differ; Orthodox Jews generally affirm resurrection while many Reform Jews emphasize the soul and memory
The Torah describes heaven in detail
Judaism has never discussed life after death
test.why: Rabbinic Judaism taught resurrection; the Reform movement set bodily resurrection aside in 1885.

test.q: In Islamic teaching, what happens on the Day of Judgment?
choices: All are raised, their deeds weighed, and they enter paradise or hell
The dead become ancestors at family shrines
test.why: The Qur'an teaches bodily resurrection, the weighing of deeds, and entry into jannah or jahannam.

test.q: Which tradition teaches rebirth but denies a permanent soul?
test.why: Buddhism teaches anatta, non-self, while still teaching rebirth driven by karma.

choices: As a fine matter that sticks to the soul
test.why: Jains describe karma as subtle matter that clings to the jiva and is removed by nonviolence and discipline.

test.q: What answer does the Book of Job give to the friends who say suffering is punishment?
choices: It rejects their answer and sides with Job
It says suffering is caused by craving
It says Job's ancestors were to blame
test.why: At the end of Job, God says the friends have not spoken rightly, as Job has.

test.q: Which pair matches a mourning practice to its tradition?
choices: Cremation and a full reading of scripture: Sikhism
test.why: Sikhs usually cremate and hold a complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib; shiva is Jewish and burial facing Mecca is Muslim.

test.q: What is the fairest way to compare two traditions' answers to the same question?
choices: Rank them from best to worst
Compare one's highest ideal with the other's worst failure
Attribute each answer to its text and show its reasons and inner variety
Summarize both as saying the same thing
test.why: The unit's method is to describe, attribute, show variety within a tradition and compare like with like, without ranking.

write.prompt: Choose one question from this unit: What is a good life? What is justice? What happens when we die? Why is there suffering? Cite at least three texts from three different traditions (or two traditions and a secular thinker), explain what each would say and why, and show one point where they agree and one where they differ.
tips: Name each text precisely: book, chapter and verse; sura and verse; or the Dhammapada or Analects by verse or chapter.
Attribute every belief to its tradition, for example Muslims believe or according to the Gita.
Give the reason each tradition offers, not only its conclusion.
Show variety inside a tradition, such as Orthodox and Reform or Theravada and Mahayana.
Compare rather than judge, and use the unit's terms, like dharma, samsara and theodicy, correctly.
